query: High-entropy alloys contain five or more elements at 5–35 at% each, generally with comparable atomic radii. Refractory and nickel-based high-entropy alloys have demonstrated elevated-temperature mechanical properties comparable to titanium- and nickel-based alloys used in extreme environments because of their heat resistance and specific strength. However, prior investigations have mainly treated titanium and nickel as additions, leaving alloys in which both are primary constituents unexplored. Subject to the stated compositional definition, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy relative to the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted relative outcome, composition and operating boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a controlled minor addition of aluminum (around 3–5 at%) during synthesis will promote the formation of coherent γ’ precipitates in a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy, thereby enhancing its elevated-temperature mechanical properties compared to the alloy without aluminum.
generation.material_initial_state: A Ti-Ni primary high-entropy alloy composed mainly of titanium and nickel in near-equiatomic ratios (with other elements present to meet the HEA definition) and without aluminum addition.
generation.intervention: Incorporate a controlled addition of approximately 3–5 at% aluminum during alloy synthesis.
generation.conditions: Alloy synthesis under conditions ensuring homogenous mixing followed by heat treatments at elevated temperatures (approximately 800–1100°C) to enable γ’ precipitate formation; subsequent mechanical tests (e.g., tensile or creep tests) at these elevated temperatures.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a coherent, ordered γ’ precipitate phase within the Ti-Ni based solid-solution matrix.
generation.mechanism: The added Al induces the precipitation of a γ’ phase that impedes dislocation motion and enhances creep resistance, thereby delivering improved yield strength and thermal stability at elevated temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: The aluminum-modified alloy is expected to exhibit significantly higher high-temperature yield strength and creep resistance relative to the baseline Ti-Ni HEA lacking Al, due to the precipitation strengthening effect of the coherent γ’ phase.
generation.baseline: The same titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy processed identically but without the aluminum addition.
generation.boundary: The improvement is anticipated only within a specific aluminum concentration range (around 3–5 at%) and under processing conditions that prevent the formation of unwanted brittle intermetallics; also limited by the operational temperature range (approximately 800–1100°C) where the γ’ phase remains stable.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the improvement is uncertain and will depend on precise Al content, processing parameters, and the nature of the overall HEA composition; if too much aluminum is added, deleterious phases may form.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloys: one baseline Ti-Ni primary HEA without aluminum, and one with a controlled 3–5 at% Al addition. Process both under identical synthesis and heat treatment conditions designed to promote uniform microstructures. Characterize the microstructure using transmission electron microscopy (TEM) for precipitate identification and phase determination. Conduct high-temperature mechanical testing (tensile and creep tests) in the range of 800–1100°C.
measurements: Quantification of γ’ precipitate volume fraction and coherence via TEM and X-ray diffraction (XRD).
Yield strength and creep resistance measurements at elevated temperatures.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-added alloy fails to exhibit a statistically significant improvement (e.g., less than a 10% increase) in yield strength or creep resistance at elevated temperatures compared to the baseline, or if TEM/XRD analyses do not detect the formation of coherent γ’ precipitates, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractHigh-entropy alloys (HEAs) have drawn significant attention due to their unique design and superior mechanical properties. Comprising 5–35 at% of five or more elements with similar atomic radii, HEAs exhibit high configurational entropy, resulting in single-phase solid solutions rather than intermetallic compounds. Additive manufacturing (AM), particularly direct energy deposition (DED), is effective for producing HEAs due to its rapid cooling rates, which ensure uniform microstructures and minimize defects. These alloys typically form face-centered cubic (FCC) or body-centered cubic (BCC) structures, contributing to their exceptional strength, hardness, and mechanical performance across various temperatures. However, FCC-structured HEAs often have low yield strengths, posing a challenge for structural applications. In this study, a Ni-Co-Fe-Cr-Al-Ti HEA was manufactured using the DED method. This study proposes that the addition of aluminum and titanium creates a γ + γ′ phase structure within a multicomponent FCC-HEA matrix, enhancing the thermal stability and coarsening the resistance and strength. High-entropy alloys (HEAs) have gained considerable attention due to their innovative design and outstanding mechanical properties []. HEAs consist of 5~35 at% of five or more elements with similar atomic radii, resulting in high configurational entropy, significant lattice distortion, and reduced diffusion rates []. HEAs are typically characterized by configurational entropies exceeding 1.5R (where R is the gas constant) []. The configurational entropy equation is shown in Equation (1). where Δsmix is the constituent entropy, N is the number of elements, and xi is the entropy of each element. Due to their high entropy, HEAs tend to form single-phase solid solutions rather than intermetallic compounds. This unique composition and microstructure give HEAs exceptional mechanical properties. HEAs generally exhibit a single-phase face-centered cubic (FCC) or body-centered cubic (BCC) structure []. Unlike typical alloys, HEAs form a concentrated solid solution. Consequently, HEAs exhibit high strength and hardness at room temperature, along with excellent mechanical performance at both low and high temperatures [].

reading.lever: Introduce a controlled Al addition during synthesis to form coherent γ’ precipitates within a Ti-Ni high-entropy matrix.
reading.why: This strategy leverages a proven precipitation-strengthening mechanism from related Ni-containing HEAs to improve high-temperature mechanical properties in Ti-Ni systems.
